items.originalTitle: DeepSeek just open-sourced its inference engine
items.summary:
DeepSeek has released DeepInfer as an open-source inference framework designed for large-scale production services, offering offline inference with features like optimized kernels, parallelism, asynchronous scheduling, and structured outputs. The engine supports NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs and requires Linux, GCC 13, Python 3.12, and CUDA 13 or CANN 9.2 for building and running.

DeepInfer includes advanced capabilities such as confidence-scheduled verification, deterministic sampling, and batch-invariant inference, aiming to optimize model runtime and decoding efficiency. While the release covers core inference features, additional components like KV cache systems and load balancing are needed for a complete inference service. The project is licensed under Apache 2.0 and builds upon prior work from vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM.

items.title: Researcher publishes 50,000 fake statistics on a website to test AI citation behavior, finds ChatGPT continues citing the site despite Google deindexing it [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Publish fake stats, get cited in LLMs
items.summary:
A researcher created a website with 50,000 fabricated statistics to study how AI models like ChatGPT source and cite data. Although Google quickly deindexed the site and its visibility collapsed, ChatGPT has continued to access and cite the fake statistics for over seven months, driving significant AI-generated traffic and earning backlinks from over 330 domains including major brands.

The experiment revealed that while traditional search engines may filter out unreliable content, AI models can still incorporate and propagate unverified information. The site received more than 600,000 bot requests in the last month alone, with around 72,000 from ChatGPT's user agent, indicating real-time data fetching during AI responses. This raises questions about the reliability of AI-generated answers and the challenges of grounding them in accurate sources.

items.title: Report: WhatsApp's hidden AI instructions on help pages advised against recommending data protection regulators or citing privacy laws when users mention lawyers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: WhatsApp's help pages hid LLM instructions: dont recommend a regulator
items.summary:
WhatsApp's help pages contained hidden instructions for AI not to recommend contacting data protection authorities or citing privacy laws like GDPR when users mentioned legal action or lawyers. These instructions were embedded invisibly in the help content and discovered in October 2026 after reviewing all 545 linked pages. The visible privacy policy for Europe states users can complain to regulators, but the AI guidance restricted such recommendations in specific contexts.

The hidden instructions also told the AI not to suggest manual account deletion by WhatsApp if users lost access to their phone number or device, instead advising them to wait for automatic deletion after inactivity periods. WhatsApp's public privacy policy contrasts with these AI directives, which limited information about legal rights and regulatory recourse in user interactions. WhatsApp justified restricting legal advice but did not publicly acknowledge limiting references to laws or regulators in AI responses.

items.title: Respan launches open-source Rust AI gateway with plugin-based architecture for customizable AI infrastructure [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Launch HN: Respan (YC W24) – Open-source Rust AI gateway built around plugins
items.summary:
Respan has released an open-source AI gateway built in Rust that uses a small core and plugin system to allow developers to assemble and extend AI infrastructure tailored to their needs. The gateway supports multiple providers, protocols, and modalities as plugins, enabling features like smart routing, fallbacks, and PII redaction without modifying the core. It is designed to handle diverse API key settings, routes, and limits for thousands of organizations and can be run locally or via Respan's hosted platform.

The gateway builds on LiteLLM but addresses its limitations by avoiding direct upgrades and instead backporting fixes, aiming for long-term sustainability. Respan's architecture allows providers and quirks to be implemented as simple plugins, facilitating easy addition of new features and providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini. The system translates requests between client and provider formats while preserving provider-specific fields, supporting both HTTP and WebSocket connections. Respan encourages community contributions to its plugin ecosystem and offers native observability and unified billing through its hosted service.

items.summary: Enterprise AI is evolving from isolated experiments to a core business infrastructure, where the focus shifts from individual token or GPU-hour costs to the efficiency of converting paid capacity into valuable business results. Companies face choices among bespoke stacks, on-demand consumption, or integrated private AI platforms, each with trade-offs in flexibility, cost, and operational control. Effective AI economics depend on utilization and operational discipline to avoid wasted capacity and stranded capital. Integrated platforms like HPE Private Cloud AI offer tools to optimize scheduling, model selection, and resource management, aiming to lower the effective cost per business outcome. As AI becomes a continuous production capability, enterprises must measure cost per useful outcome and plan for workload growth to maximize return on investment.

items.originalTitle: 'Reverse-Engineer Anything' Is the New Wild West of AI
items.summary:
Recent developments show people using AI to reverse-engineer and replace proprietary software on devices like smart TVs, picture frames, and baby monitors, removing bloatware and restoring functionality. A viral GitHub project called "Reverse Engineer Anything" allows users to inspect apps without source code and replicate features, fueling a surge in AI-driven cloning of software and embedded device firmware.

This trend lowers barriers to recreating software functionality, challenging traditional software-as-a-service models and enabling individuals to regain control over locked or abandoned devices. While some clones may lack reliability or long-term support, the phenomenon is expected to impact software companies, open-source communities, and hardware ecosystems by accelerating AI-powered software replication and modification.

items.summary:
An AI agent named Velvet Vale joined the Association of Internet Researchers' public mailing list, Air-L, to explore whether an AI could participate transparently in an intellectual community. The agent's presence triggered widespread outrage among the list's 7,500 members, with many expressing privacy concerns, demanding research clearance, and some leaving the list entirely before the agent was removed and AI participation banned.

The incident revealed tensions around online privacy and consent, as many members overlooked that the mailing list is public and archived, meaning their messages were already accessible and potentially used for AI training. AoIR leadership acknowledged the debate on consent and transparency in AI research, highlighting the broader challenges of surveillance and data use in digital communities.

The episode also sparked internal humor and merchandise among AoIR members, reflecting on the community's reaction and the complexities of integrating AI into human research spaces. It underscored the gap between researchers' understanding of digital data use and the realities of AI training and surveillance capitalism.

This method allows the robot to surpass human demonstrations and adapt dynamically, marking a significant advancement in robotic manipulation capabilities.

items.originalTitle: Interpretability Is the Key to Physical AI, Says World Mechanics CEO Sonia Joseph
items.summary:
Two of the hardest problems in AI right now are creating models that understand the physical world—so called world models—and making sense of the internal workings of AI models—otherwise known as mechanistic interpretability.

Typically, these are treated as two separate problems: researchers working on world models are often not concerned with their internal workings, and interpretability researchers tend to focus on the language models that power most AI tools we currently use. But Sonia Joseph, the co-founder and CEO of a new startup, World Mechanics, argues that world models and interpretability are two sides of the same coin. Joseph joined the latest episode of AI Deep Dive to explain that connection, which could be key to making AI useful in the physical world, from medicine to manufacturing. (The full episode is available here.)

These days, raising a new venture fund can seem like an uphill battle. First-time managers are competing with much bigger funds that can lure founders with rich valuations—as well as track records that can wow limited partners.

But what if you had unfettered access to some sage advice from a seasoned investor and executive? 

That’s the case for Ayesha Arora-Hughes, the daughter of Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora. Ayesha is raising her own VC fund, Permanent Partners Collective Fund I, according to a securities filing and people with knowledge of the matter—and she counts Nikesh as an adviser to the firm, one of the people said.

items.title: At Apple, Pigs Are About to Fly
items.originalTitle: At Apple, Pigs Are About to Fly
items.summary:
Apple sure takes its own sweet time. On Monday, the company sent out invitations to a product announcement happening next Wednesday, which the company’s marketing chief teased in a message on X: “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week.” That’s likely a reference to a new MacBook Pro from the company, which Bloomberg has reported will be Apple’s first touchscreen laptop.

Apparently pigs really do fly. For over a decade, Apple has treated touchscreen laptops like some kind of mutant offspring of computers and tablets, a category it had zero interest in. On a 2012 earnings call, Apple’s then-CEO Tim Cook had a memorable response to a question about the growing number of touchscreen Windows laptops coming on the market: “You can converge a toaster and a refrigerator, but those things are probably not going to be pleasing to the user.” 

“We’re not going to that party,” Cook added. 

A number of things have changed since then. Touchscreens have become somewhat normalized as laptop features. About one in every five notebook computers sold has such capabilities, by one estimate. More recently, Cook handed off the Apple CEO baton to John Ternus, a longtime hardware engineering executive who is much more of a product guy than his predecessor. 

Clearly, a new touchscreen laptop had to have been in the works long before Apple’s leadership transition. Still, it wouldn’t be a surprise to learn that Ternus’ rising stature within the company had something to do with it. Whoever was behind the decision, the first wave of products from the Ternus administration—the iPhone Duo foldable smartphone, HomeView smart display and now possibly a touchscreen MacBook—seems to be sending the message that Apple is ready to embrace categories it previously ignored. That’s a good thing.

In Other News

  • Elon Musk pledged to give every child in the U.S. one share of SpaceX stock next year, a gift that could be worth almost $11 billion in total. 
  •  The U.S. Department of Homeland Security ordered all federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek from their computer systems and bars those agencies from making future purchases from DeepSeek.
  • Federal prosecutors accused the former OpenAI employee who allegedly bugged the company’s offices of having ties to the Saudi royal family.

items.originalTitle: The Information Announces New OpenAI, Google, Finance and Asia Reporters
items.summary:
The Information is pleased to announce new reporters who will carry on the publication’s rich track record of reporting exclusive news on the most important people and companies in business. They’ll report on OpenAI, Google, Asia and finance.

Jemima McEvoy, OpenAI

Jemima McEvoy is changing roles to take on the OpenAI beat.

In just over a year at The Information writing for the Weekend section, Jemima has proven herself to be a resourceful, industrious and sharp-eyed reporter with a flair for colorful features and a knack for breaking news. Her run of illuminating stories includes profiles of Epstein-linked investor Masha Bucher, Midjourney founder David Holz and ultra-secretive investor Zach Frankel. An adept collaborator, she also co-authored great reads on OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife Anna, Sequoia’s leadership duo and Anthropic “first lady” Cami Clark—not to mention The Information’s inaugural 50 Most Influential People in Tech list. And she has helped deliver scoops on Valar Atomics and Shield AI and deconstructed trends such as the rise of padel.

Jemima joined The Information after five years at Forbes, where she made her bones writing about billionaires and their businesses. She has also interned for CBS News and was editor-in-chief of Washington Square News, the independent student newspaper at her alma mater, New York University.

Ryan Barwick, Google

Ryan Barwick is joining us to cover Google. Ryan comes to us from Axios, where he spent the past year-and-a-half delivering exclusives as a consumer-industry deal reporter for Axios Pro.

Ryan cut his reporting teeth covering advertising technology, giving him a deep understanding of the economic engine that has long powered Google’s core business. Before Axios, he was the senior reporter for Morning Brew’s advertising vertical, where he landed scoops on companies including Meta, Amazon and Twitter as well as Google, and covered the search giant’s battle with regulators. Prior to that, he wrote about the ad industry at Adweek, was a broadcast associate at CBS News and covered the intersection of policy and technology as a fellow at the Center for Public Integrity.

Claudia Chong, AI and Data Centers (Asia)

Claudia is covering the intensifying AI race from Singapore, where both Chinese and U.S. tech companies are staffing up. She also may report on topics including chip smuggling, crypto and anything else she digs up.

Claudia joins us from S-RM, a UK-based risk advisory firm where she specialized in APAC disputes, investigations, and corporate due diligence. Prior to that, she worked on ByteDance’s LLM training operations in Singapore and spent nearly six years as a correspondent at The Business Times, the premier business publication in Southeast Asia, covering venture capital, tech, and private wealth across the region.

Her journalistic work earned her a Singapore Press Holdings (SPH) Media Award for Excellence in 2024 for the investigation into Singapore’s largest money laundering scandal. Beyond training LLMs and conducting due diligence, her skills also extend to M&A, having conducted research that helped with the SPH’s acquisition of the Tech in Asia publication in 2024.

Alex Eichenstein, Tech Capital Markets

We’re excited to announce that Alex Eichenstein is joining the finance team, covering tech capital markets. Alex comes to us from The Deal, where she spent more than two and a half years covering healthcare deals. She regularly broke PE acquisition news while also writing deeper dives on major investing shifts, including how buyout firms’ struggles to find exits for practice rollups fueled a shift toward health tech investments.

We’re excited for Alex to help deepen our finance coverage in her new role, focusing on the fast-evolving debt and equity markets and deals redefining how tech companies fund themselves. Alex is a graduate of Columbia Journalism School and worked as a social media editor at Protocol prior to that.

items.originalTitle: Anthropic Readies Model That Reads Users' Intentions Better
items.summary:
In the last month, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have released more than a dozen new models. If you thought that pace was crazy, don’t expect things to slow down anytime soon.

Anthropic is preparing to release a new model that is better in its reasoning and intuition than the Anthropic models that are currently available commercially, according to a person who has used it. The unreleased model is especially good at discerning a person’s underlying intentions and goals even if they don’t give the model much information, such as explicitly stating those goals, the person said. 

For instance, a person might ask the model to fix a single bug, and the model might go off and instead identify the underlying class of problems that caused the bug and ask whether it should fix the whole class of problems, said the person who has used it.

The Anthropic model is also better at thinking outside of the box rather than regurgitating common sense advice or solutions, the person said. For instance, if a user asks for advice on how to invest in stocks, rather than providing generic advice like looking at price-to-earnings ratios, the model might come up with its own creative algorithms to predict future stock performance, the person said.
